utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I invite the Defence to call its next witness, I'd like to deal with a few procedural issues as well. It will presumably not take much time. The first issue is the expert report of the expert Radovanovic that has been presented later than the other expert reports. The Prosecution usually has a certain period of time in order to express itself on whether it accepts the report or not. That time has not yet elapsed. Could the Prosecution inform the Chamber whether they would be in a position to express themselves on the acceptance or non-acceptance of that report in an earlier stage than provided by the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we could do that on Monday, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would also appreciate if the Prosecution could by then indicate how much time they would need to prepare for cross-examination, if they would not accept the report. Of course this all independent yet from whether the report will be admitted into evidence as not. But the Chamber has found no reasons at this moment to decide that it would not admit the report into evidence. Then another issue is a request from the Defence to reconsider a decision taken by the Chamber. The -- in the situation in which the Defence expressed that it had not made up its mind yet as to whether it would call the accused to testify, the Chamber gave an order in respect of some procedural aspects in case the Defence would decide to call the accused. These aspects, for example, were the chronological order, including a possible re-call of the witness and disclosure in order to provide the Prosecution with information they would need to prepare for cross-examination. The Defence sought a certificate for an appeal against this order. The Chamber has denied this request. And the Defence has subsequently requested the Chamber to reconsider its order. Where the Defence has neither indicated that the position of the Defence differs from the situation in which the order was given nor has based its present request on newly adduced legal arguments, the Chamber considers that in these circumstances there's no need to decide on the matter. These were the procedural issues the Chamber needed to address. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the Defence calls the next witness, I think we are still to tender -- we have still to tender the exhibits from the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, from the last witness. And as far as I'm aware of, we have one document that should be marked for identification, I think. That's the list -- the witness has provided the list with the names on it. Madam Usher -- Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since there are no objections, the document is admitted into evidence. Then we have as a remaining -- we have still to give it a number, yes. Mr. Ierace, admitting a document into evidence without a P number could create confusion. Could you provide us with a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you may think it over what number you'd think suitable, and we'll hear from you then. Meanwhile, I do understand that there is some confusion as -- Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: P3784, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3784 is then admitted into evidence. We have some problems in respect -- with respect to the videotapes being played. They do bear a P number, as far as I understand, but the Chamber, assisted by the registrar, had some difficulties in finding the moment where this video had been played before, at what moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Madam Registrar has solved our problem.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The three videotapes that were played were P3280Q, under seal; P3280P; and P3280S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand that they were all admitted already in evidence. Just for the record that these were the videos that have been played. If there's no other issue to be dealt with at this very moment, I'd like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps a problem. Mr. President, we still don't know whether a number has to be given to the expert report or not, since it has been provided as an expert report. I don't know where we stand with regard to this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll inform you as soon as -- we have to reconsider it. The issue has been brought to our attention. It's not urgent at this moment. We can proceed without an immediate decision. So we'll give it in due course. Then, Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to call its next witness? And that would be, as far as I understand, Elena Guskova?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Guskova, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I am informed that you would be willing to make that solemn declaration in the English language. There's nothing against it. But if you would prefer to do it in your own language, I'll ask the interpreters to translate it for you. So I'll leave it up to you whether you make the declaration in, as far as I understand, Russian, your native language, or in English, just as you prefer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have the English text, then I can do it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... It's being handed out to you now by the usher. May I then invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. I have to warn you. If you don't put the headphone really on your head, it will fall off again and again according to our experience, so... Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Guskova, good day.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start asking you questions, could you please tell us what your full name is and could you tell us where you work and what your profession is.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: My last name is Guskova. The first name, Elena. My father's name is Yuri. So in Russian it is Elena Yuryevna. I am a specialist in the history of Yugoslav peoples. In 1971, I graduated from the history of south and west Slavs at the Moscow State University, and my specialty is the history of Yugoslavia. As of 1973, in the academy of sciences I have been studying the modern Yugoslavia, that is, after -- post 1945, even though my doctoral dissertation covered the nineteenth century. When crisis broke out in Yugoslavia, the academy of sciences, that is, the Centre for Slavonic Studies, a centre was set up to study the modern Yugoslav crisis and I have been the head of the department for the past ten years. It is the only centre in the world which engages in scientific research of developments in the Balkans. We approach the subject in very strict scientific terms. So I continued to investigate these matters. In 1994, I worked as a scientific expert with the blue helmets headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Guskova, since you told us that you worked as the director of the centre for researching the contemporary crisis in the Balkans at the Russian Academy of Science, can you tell us whether you have been involved in other matters as well, and what is your profession in relation to your scientific work and your research work?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I'm a doctor of history. I also teach, and I teach history of the Balkan crisis at the faculty of history and at the academy for diplomats.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Guskova, you provided us with a statement in response to the Defence request, and you dealt with the crisis period in Yugoslavia, and you focussed in particular on Sarajevo, that is to say, on Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the light of international factors, was that the subject of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes. And my expert opinion covered the beginning of the crisis and the part that the international factor played in that crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Guskova, you have told us that in 1994, as far as I have understood you, you were present as a UN official. Can you be more precise and tell us how you were engaged and which areas were you present in from 1994 as a UN official.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: In 1994, I was invited -- I received an invitation from Washington to participate in the group of experts in Mr. Akashi's office as a Balkan specialist. The fact is that when Yasushi Akashi was assigned to the high office of the personal representative of the Secretary-General, he was the only one who realised that in his cabinet there were no Balkanologists. There were diplomats. There were military, vast numbers of journalists, but very few specialists. And that was why an expert group was set up. And this group of experts was made practically of three individuals: Susan Woodward from the United States was its head. And apart from me, there was yet another young colleague from Italy. They found me on the basis of my published papers. By now I have published over 230 papers on the subject. In answer to a question, being at such a high office, as a deputy head of the experts, I had the opportunity to indeed use all the possible resources in order to acquaint myself with the situation in the Balkans. We had at our disposal, helicopters, cars, and also we had the possibility to visit all possible areas, including the hot spots. I was there from April to October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Guskova. But I think that I didn't quite understand something. You said "in the Balkans." I didn't quite understand where your headquarters were located and where you were as a member of that group.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: We were in Zagreb, at the headquarters of the UNPROFOR, on the same floor but different wing from Mr. Yasushi Akashi's cabinet. Our task was to prepare expert opinions for the negotiations that were to take place or the developments that were taking place. Another task of our group was to brief the arriving officers, diplomats, members of the mission in the ex-Yugoslav territory about the situation, about the history, that is, and the current situation in the Balkans. And I can tell you one interesting fact in this regard. Throughout --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait for the witness to finish her answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Please finish your answer and then I'll put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Only one man arrived who wanted to know what was going on in the Balkans, and he was a military officer from Africa.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Guskova, bearing in mind the report that you compiled at the Defence's request, could you tell us - and you have already told us where you worked. You said that you worked in an institute - could you tell us what sources you used when writing your report. What did you base your report on?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I wrote my analysis many years -- after many years of my scientific research and researches conducted my theme [as interpreted] in the centre for the study of the Yugoslav crisis, and we had a large collection of documents about these developments. We've already published six volumes of documents relative to these developments, including some international documents, so that my expertise was based on the documents of international organisations. Apart from that, all the possible available literature that we had we also studied. And yet another type of sources which has begun to emerge of late, and that is the memories of people who served in the Balkans and now have been relieved of their duties and are therefore able to publicise -- to reveal their personal perception of the developments. I also had the opportunity to meet a number of political leaders of parties to the conflict, their military representatives, and also rank and file people whom I interviewed. I have the recordings of these interviews, though not all, unfortunately, because some people would not authorise these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have now told us which documents you used. Can you tell us, in your opinion what are the main reasons for the crisis in the territory of the former Yugoslavia? But since time is restricted, I would like to ask you to tell us about these reasons that led to the crisis very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: As a rule, the error made by those who studied the crisis in the Balkans now is that they do not go into the whole set of the causes of the crisis. But there is no time for me to go into that, so I shall give you the basic conclusion of my studies. It seems that the chief reason is the relationship between the internal and the external factor in the emergence of the crisis, its escalation, and the break-up of Yugoslavia. The internal factors were an important condition. But the external factor became the fundamental in the disintegration of the Federation and the escalation of the crisis. If we talk about internal factors, then no doubt the chief engine, the chief driving force of the process --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Guskova, in order to be clearer, my question is: In your opinion, what are the internal causes of the conflict? Could you tell us about the internal causes very briefly, and then I will ask you about the external ones.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: With regard to the internal reasons, a major role was played by the historical -- by historical factors. And I really realised that the parties who tried to resolve the matter did not take it into mind. The economic, sociological, ideological and all the other factors, they are all very important. But the driving force behind all these processes was the aspiration of the countries to independence, first Slovenia and Croatia followed by Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the desire to secede, the desire of the republics and the territory of the former Yugoslavia to secede -- and you also included Bosnia and Herzegovina in this. In your opinion, what was the reason for the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Every historical events have causes which are more removed or immediate causes. The immediate cause was perhaps the sequence of events. If we take every event separately, every one of these events, of these incidents is important. However, we're interested in the consequences of these events. For instance, in February 1991, at that time the negotiations amongst the six leaders of the republics were just beginning about the future of the Federation, and at that time already the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina already had on its agenda the declaration of independence. At that time the -- well, it was not adopted, but those who knew what was going on were already quite clear what it meant. In April 1991, there were still negotiations underway about the future of Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were already preparations underway for the establishment of armed formations, notably the Patriotic League, Green Berets, and the Muslim Youth. And this was in April. Then further events unfolded, so that Bosnia-Herzegovina proposed its own -- made its proposal regarding the future Yugoslavia. It became quite clear that it did not -- it was not particularly keen on remaining Yugoslavia any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please slow down a bit because the interpreters have to interpret every single word you say so that we can take full knowledge of your testimony. And they have some difficulties with your speed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then in June --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Guskova, please just speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I shall be happy to do that. In June 1991, whilst the negotiations among the leaders of the six republics were not yet finished, nevertheless Alija Izetbegovic set up his National Defence Council, the tasks which were to prepare the defence of the republic. All these factors naturally played a major role and contributed to an atmosphere of uncertainty, at least in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- although in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although, the majority of people in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not believe that the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina could deteriorate. Then if we continue considering the events of 1991, there were still no serious signs that the conflict was afoot, but it is very also -- the very important date for us is the 12th October 1991, which is the well-known assembly -- the well-known session of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina which adopted the memorandum on independence in the absence of the representatives of one of the peoples. And then, as early as January 1992, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina put on the agenda the organisation of a referendum on independence. And then it became quite clear that the positions were already taken and that Bosnia-Herzegovina would aspire to achieve its independence. It was very important then to solve the question concerning the future of that republic. I haven't mentioned some very important dates, and those were the proclamation of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the recognition by international organisations. This is a very interesting moment -- it is interesting how they publicised independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then the mobilisation of the 4th of April. All these events added momentum to the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Guskova. You say that all these events made the crisis worse in that area. Can you tell us what the outcome of that crisis was.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The outcome of the crisis was armed conflict. That was the final upshot. I'm not talking about different stages of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that it was an armed conflict. Can you tell us which parties were involved in that armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina - and I believe you know that - there were three sides which had part in it. But I suppose the most important thing is to see what was the -- what were the objectives of the belligerents or parties to the conflict because they pursued different objectives and had different tasks ahead. They also strived to solve them in different ways. So Muslims - and I call them Muslims, meaning an ethnic group - and I apologise, but that is how it happens in the history of Yugoslavia. In 1961, then in 1971 in Bosnia-Herzegovina the Muslims wrote, "Ethnicity: Muslim faith". This is just by way of clarification. So the Muslims were trying to keep an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent republic, as an independent state, indispensable, which would not be part of Yugoslavia any longer. The other side - and I'd say that this is perhaps the most interesting question which often puzzles those who study the situation in the former Yugoslavia - and that is the question what was the Serbs' objective. The Serbs originally did not want to leave Yugoslavia. That sentiment and that desire to stay in Yugoslavia, to keep Yugoslavia in one piece, was something that all Serbs professed, be they in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Kosovo, or Macedonia. And therefore, the primary task of the Serbs was to try to stay within Yugoslavia. And only later on the objectives began to change when it became clear that the conflict would break out with regard to the future of the Federation and the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then the task set was to try to protect and keep the territories of the Serb population, and in that form, if possible, to then join Yugoslavia. However, even later, when it became clear that Yugoslavia was not supporting the unification of the Serb lands...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Thank you. Mrs. Guskova, I would now like to ask you, given the fact that you have already told us which were the sides to that conflict. Now, can you tell us how did that conflict reflect to your mind in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in more specific terms in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Do you want me to finish with all the three parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But I believe that you have already told us -- actually, you mentioned two sides. Can you please tell us which was the third side and then answer my previous question.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Two parties, yes. Yes, of course. Well, the Serb objectives changed because then they said that they wanted their own territories at least within Bosnia-Herzegovina, if Yugoslavia would not take them in. The third party were Croats, who vacillated in that situation because they were incapable of conducting an independent policy concerning Bosnia-Herzegovina and within Bosnia-Herzegovina and were coordinating fully their plans with the Republic of Croatia. So this would be briefly in answer to your previous question. As to the developments, how the -- what kind of developments took place in Sarajevo, well, it was pretty turbulent. Things were unfolding rather fast. After March and especially after April 1992, this city was partitioned along the ethnic lines, and this then gave rise -- this was the cause of what happened directly in the city of Sarajevo and about which we are only now beginning to get more or less reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Guskova, you have told us that Sarajevo was divided on ethnic principles, and you have also told us that already in March there was a conflict in that area. Can you also tell us whether there was an attempt to stop that conflict, both internally as well as externally. And who was it who tried to stop this conflict internally and who was it who tried to stop it externally? But again, if I could ask you to give us a short answer. I know that it is very difficult for you to give us short answers. These are complex questions. But let's try and be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I apologise if I'm not brief enough, but this is the subject of my scientific research and I always feel the need to explain in-depth what I know. My course of lectures includes 50 hours, and I find it very difficult to restrict myself, confine it. Will you please remind me of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any attempts to stop the conflict, both internal attempts and external attempts? So can you please tell us who was it internally who tried to stop the conflict, to your mind, that is.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: First of all, internally speaking it was the citizens who were making these attempts. There were many layers, or rather, many attempts at various layers of society to stop the conflict. In mid-May we had peaceful demonstrations when the entire city was out in the streets trying to stop the already obvious wave of the conflict. In April, after mobilisation was called, all the citizens turned off the lights in their apartments as a sign of protests. That was the way they expressed their attitude towards the conflict. There was also an attempt by the people who were opposed to Alija Izetbegovic, I mean among the Muslims. They also attempted to stop the oncoming conflict. That was the historical agreement suggested by Zulfikarpasic to Alija Izetbegovic. Externally speaking, without any doubt, the intervention of international organisations was another attempt to stop this conflict. It was also a many-layered, multi-fold intervention and had many expressions, was expressed in different terms and used different methods.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Guskova, you have now told us that as far as the attempts to stop the conflict are concerned that there was a rally of citizens in Sarajevo. And you have also told us that there were attempts by the people in the leadership of Alija Izetbegovic to stop that conflict. Were there any other internal elements who tried to stop the conflicts? If you have any knowledge of that, if you have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Do you mean internally? I have already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, internally.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Those were attempts to reach an agreement - I wish to underline this again - among the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you mention the interparty agreement, can you please tell us which was the other party that tried to reach some sort of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Well, if I understand your question correctly, the Serb side for its part tried to stop the conflict as well, but that was already linked to the activity of international organisations. Serbs have done a great deal to prevent the conflict, at least in the region of Sarajevo and the Sarajevo airport. But that was already within the framework of the negotiation process headed by international organisations and the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I will come back to international organisations and the Security Council. But now I have a question for you. When you were studying all these documents and preparing the report on the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, can you please tell us what was the role of the Yugoslav People's Army during that period? And the period that I have in mind is during the year 1992 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Well, as far as the role of the Yugoslav People's Army is concerned, I believe we should be speaking primarily about year 1992, because it was -- because preceding from the experience of the JNA in Croatia, based on that experience the JNA was reluctant to get involved in the conflict. After the first barricades put up in the streets, after the 1st of March, 1992, and after the agreement reached between Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, and the Croat representatives on taking down these barricades, the JNA took part in this agreement and it attempted to make a buffer zone and tried not to get involved in what was going on in the streets of Sarajevo, because the consequences were going to be very serious and the leadership of the JNA was aware of this. Within the JNA, serious movements were already going on towards changing the internal structure because all the soldiers and officers who were ethnic Muslims were already leaving the army in 1992. This process had begun already in spring 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Guskova, in your reply you have also mentioned the role of international organisations and the Security Council in the attempt to resolve the conflict in the area of Sarajevo. Can you please tell us, how did international organisations try to solve this problem and what international organisations those were?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Allow me at the outset to make one conclusion that we reached while studying the entire process of finding a settlement in the Balkans; that is the following: Stopping the crisis was possible at each stage of its development, beginning with 1991. However, this was not done and all attempts failed. And one of the reasons is that in the Balkans we saw an intersection of various interests, a clash of various interests and various methods of resolving the crisis. First of all, there was the European Union, which developed its own system for reaching a settlement. This system included the headquarters of blue helmets, which also took part in the process of negotiations. Then there were foreign ministers of many countries who were promoting the interests of their own countries and kept commuting between Belgrade, Sarajevo, and Zagreb, also taking part in negotiations. Then another segment was made up of the Security Council itself. This body took it upon itself to play the legislator and create a legislative basis for resolving the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the Security Council tried to resolve the situation, can you also tell us how the Security Council tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The principal lever or tool of the Security Council were discussions, deliberations, preparation for debates on certain issues and adoption of resolutions on the Yugoslav crisis. There were several hundred resolutions on the Yugoslav crisis adopted in total by the Security Council, beginning with 1992 -- 1991 to date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that there were hundreds of resolutions, but can you tell us with regard to the year 1992 -- or from 1991 and in 1992, in your opinion what were the important resolutions in the Sarajevo area which were adopted and how were they implemented -- in the area of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: It is easy to enumerate resolutions. It is more difficult to explain how they were put in practice, because those who adopted the resolutions were inspired by the feeling of striving for justice and finding a solution. However, if we analyse the resolutions themselves, we see that as a result of actions based on these resolutions, there are two components of these actions, two interesting aspects. One, not all resolutions were possible to implement. At least the intent underlying the resolutions was not possible to achieve in practice. And secondly, the approach to the parties to the conflict was not always objective. If we cite now at least a couple of examples of resolutions that were impossible to implement, we will easily see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question in relation to Sarajevo would be: Why was it not possible to implement those resolutions? What was the reason for this? To be more precise, can you tell us which resolution was concerned in 1992 in the area of Sarajevo and what was the result of this resolution and the attempt to implement it in the territory of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: One could quote several examples. For instance, resolution 752, relative to -- and this is May 1992. If I am correct, it was the 15th of May, when it was adopted. And it dealt with the substance of the conflict and attempt to get out of the territory of Sarajevo the armed forces and from Bosnia-Herzegovina the armed forces which were illegally formed, the Yugoslav People's Army, and the Croatian army. The next resolution, 757, which mostly dealt with the sanctions. But it once again emphasised that the pulling out of the Yugoslav People's Army had started but not the Croatian army, and the Croatian army was never pulled out from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, first of all because according to the calculations, about 40 to 50 thousand of military men from Croatia supported their Croat brethren in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Guskova, bearing in mind the two resolutions, 752 and 757, that you have mentioned, what was the position with regard to these resolutions on the part of the Serbian side? So what was the attitude of the Serbian side and the JNA with regard to these two resolutions and the attempt to implement them?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The resolution 757, apart from the decision to enforce sanctions and pull out units also addressed the question of the Sarajevo airport, which the peacekeeping forces had asked to place under their control. And the leadership of the Army of Republika Srpska, which was being formed - that was May 1992 - was about to turn over the Sarajevo airport for peacekeeping tasks to the peacekeeping forces who would then control it and use it for the humanitarian relief. Moreover, on the 5th June, the Croats, Serbs, and Muslims - the military men, I mean - signed an understanding, an agreement on the Sarajevo airport stating that all the heavy weapons would be removed from the area of the Sarajevo airport and removed to a distance which would be beyond the reach of the projectiles. That was the 5th of June. But shortly after that Boutros Boutros-Ghali's report was submitted to the General Assembly, and in it he said that to their enormous regret the Serbs had handed over the airport but the two other parties had seized that opportunity to launch military operations against the Serb side. And Boutros Boutros-Ghali pointed out that something should be done to redress that situation. However, the demilitarisation, or the institution of the demilitarised zone in the area of the Sarajevo airport and the city its never took place. There are very many interesting moments which have to do with the Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague shall continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We have often heard about the term "aggression" or about an aggressor in this conflict. What could you tell us very briefly about this subject, the subject of aggression and the subject of aggressors.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: When the question is put as to how should one define the nature of the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is precisely then that one comes across the die that we often come across in the general -- in the press, in the media, and in the political parlance. The problem is that the definition of the nature of the conflict that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina - am I too loud? - the nature of the conflict can be easily defined. But for that one has to see which driving forces were involved in that conflict. Serbs, just like Croats, just like Muslims, are the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the term "aggression" cannot be applied to them. The Yugoslav People's Army was pulled out from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in May 1992, and therefore the -- only the Croatian army was an external - if I may call it that - factor. And that perhaps could be the reason to call this an international conflict. That is not a sufficient reason, because the things that happened there were internal, civil matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for having slowed down, but as time is restricted and if this is not a problem for the interpreters, I think you can speak a little more rapidly but without going as fast as you were going earlier on. First of all, Professor, could you turn back to what you were talking about a minute ago, the absence of objectivity. Can you tell us very briefly, very rapidly what happened after the Clinton administration had been set up in relation to the Yugoslav problem, or to be more specific in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, please. Are you talking about non-objectivity or the role of the United States of America? Because these are two different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Let's then discuss the role of the USA, and if such was the case, the change in the position of the administration.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: When I referred to the negotiations in the territory of Yugoslavia in which many parties and many protagonists of international law took part, I also referred to different and diverse interests of different countries in that process. However, it seems to me that the most characteristic example of interference - and I would even call an aggressive interference, purely American interference - and that is the role of the United States of America in the negotiations. And it was precisely when a new administration came into place in January 1993 that a turbulent -- that the United States of America very loudly entered the stage of the negotiations regarding the -- Yugoslavia. It was at that time that the Vance-Owen plan was on the table. And as Lord Owen writes in his book, with the advent of that administration he immediately felt that America would develop its own idea of the settlement of matters in the Balkans. And since the Vance -- and accused Serbs that the -- the Serbs that the Vance-Owen plan was not adopted. But Lord Owen writes about two factors in that: A, the role of the United States of America; and secondly, the escalating conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in Central Bosnia; also, the United States of America also played a negative role in the activities and actions of the contact group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, insofar as it is possible - I know it is difficult - but I would be grateful if you could be as brief as possible. We are going to continue examining these problems at an international level. And can you tell us how many international plans there were in regard -- with regard to peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, attempts to establish such plans.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Well, let's count. There was Carrington plan --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Wait. Will you first tell us how many, without counting them all.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. How many of these plans were refused by the -- were rejected by the Muslims? I'm referring to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The Muslim side rejected two plans fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to examine a plan which is what we call the contact group plan. With regard to the psychological aspect of the presentation of this plan to the sides involved in the conflict, what can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the establishment of the contact group in 1994 marked the beginning of a completely new stage in the approach to the Balkan crisis, an absolutely new stage, new in terms of the methods it used, in terms of its participants, and the results. I do not know whether the Court is aware that the contact group is generally speaking a completely unlawful body which was not set up either by the Security Council or by any other international organisation, which engaged in solving the crisis. Nevertheless, the contact group was set up based on the decision of five countries, and the European Union opposed the establishment of that group very vehemently. And the headquarters of the blue helmets was completely unaware of the establishment of this contact group. I already worked there and we were caught by surprise when we heard about it. Nonetheless, the contact group very actively and very resolutely took certain positions and started to dictate conditions to the negotiating parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. We'll go back to that. But I would now appreciate it if you could tell us with regard to the psychological aspect -- what can you tell on the basis of your own experience? What can you tell us about the way certain plans, perhaps certain maps, were put forward, were suggested to the parties to the conflict? And what were the comments made at the time in Zagreb and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The contact group developed a completely new methodology of communication with the parties to the negotiations. To begin with, they proposed a set of maps which were to be adopted by yes or no. There were no -- there was no possibility to either add anything to those -- to the map. Moreover, I have to tell you - and this is my personal impression and the result of my personal research - many people at the blue helmet headquarters in Zagreb were confident that the map of the contact -- the maps of the contact group were drawn in such a way as to make them completely unacceptable to the Serbs, and it was then that in the contact group, and while the parties were discussed whether to accept those maps or not, the contact group meanwhile was developing a method of pressure to be brought on the parties, on several of them, Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Belgrade, Mr. Milosevic, and Pale -- that is, Karadzic. But if we -- if you look carefully, what measures were being envisaged to either encourage or punish, you will see how uneven they are in relation to these different parties. The Serbs were being threatened with sanctions, with the fact that resolution 713 on the ban to deliver weapons to the Muslims would be abolished, and also that another resolution, the resolution on the limitation -- on the limitation on the weapons that could be imported into the country would also be withdrawn, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in the six plans that you have mentioned, the contact group plan, which one was it? Which number? Which order did it appear in?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The plan of the contact group was, I guess, the fifth plan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait for the answer to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As far as the four preceding plans are concerned, what can you very briefly tell us about the Serbs' will to achieve an agreement, as far as you know? But could you be as brief as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes. The previous plan was very interesting to my mind, and it could have been quite beneficial. It is called in different ways. In literature they usually refer to it as the Stoltenberg plan. The Stoltenberg plan pursued the settlement and involving in the solution of the matters directly the Serb, the Croat, and the Muslim sides. It was characteristic that almost all the views had already been harmonised, that the Serbs had come along and the Croats and Muslims. Unfortunately Alija Izetbegovic himself did not come to Geneva when this plan was discussed. And nonetheless, there was daily communication with him by telephone, and he agreed with the plan in principle, and the plan was interesting because the territory which was divided into ethnic communities had been agreed that Bosnia-Herzegovina was given an outlet to the sea. There were no problems concerning the enclaves in Gorazde and Zepa because they were being granted large corridors, and to my knowledge the Serbs and the Croats had made a huge number of concessions to the Muslim side. As a result, the result of this plan, Alija Izetbegovic refused to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, why, if you know anything about this -- why didn't Mr. Izetbegovic and/or his counsellors want to go to the negotiations in Geneva? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic writes in his book that the thing he was afraid most of all was to find himself subjugated to Belgrade. He wanted an independent, autonomous, integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he called -- and even what he signed, he signed under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to another subject now. I'd like you to answer the following question. But yet again, as briefly as possible. It has to do with the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. Do you know whether the so-called Muslim side wanted such demilitarisation to be implemented? Do you know whether the Serbian side was in favour of it as well? What can you tell us about this matter?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Your question is closely related to the question of safety zones, safe havens that was set up by international organisations. But Sarajevo is the case apart, because safe havens were defined by a resolution somewhat later than the resolution 757. I think they were set up by resolution 758 and 839. Sarajevo, however, is mentioned in earlier resolutions. At the time when the protected zones were not yet talked about, apart from the Sarajevo airport, it was then that the plan was conceived that these areas around Sarajevo should become protected areas, and there was an agreement reached by all three parties on it. The Muslim side and the Croat side did not comply with this agreement. As for the safe havens, the five towns -- the five areas that are mentioned, even those were not provided in full, even in Boutros Boutros-Ghali's report and in some of the statements of the commanders, for Briquemont, for instance, it is said in these towns the resolution of the Security Council was not carried out and that concerned in particular Sarajevo, Brcko, and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are close to the time where we'd have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to point out -- to mention the name of Mr. Briquemont. It isn't in the transcript, Mr. President. I wanted to mention this before we had the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Before we adjourn, I'd like to inform the parties that the Chamber intends to sit more tomorrow than scheduled. That would mean that we could sit during the normal hours, that is, from 9.00 until quarter to 2.00, and then after a break until 3.00 we could sit for another half -- one hour and a half, until half past 4.00. If there are any serious objections from the parties, I'd like to know that immediately. Of course, Judge El Mahdi reminds me and of course that was included -- the parties also includes you, General Galic. If there would be -- because the Chamber is fully aware of what it asks from you, in terms of -- of problems with your back. But if there would be any serious objections, we'd like to know that as soon as possible after the break. As the parties are aware of, we'll not sit on Friday because that's court maintenance. General Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you for asking me, but I cannot really say anything because I do not know how I will feel tomorrow. It varies. On some days, I'm fine; on other days, not really. So I don't know -- so I really don't know how I will feel tomorrow. I'm trying to be honest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand. Perhaps we could follow the procedure we followed before, that as soon as you feel that you're not able to attend any more, when you feel that it would be too much, that you immediately indicate it to me. And that means that, like many things in life, this -- the final result will remain uncertain until we are there. Thank you for your observation. And if any of the parties for other reasons would not be in a position to sit for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We often discuss the subject of airports, Mr. President, and that is one of my problems. But it concerns the Schiphol airport, not the one at Dobrinja. I'll see what our plan, our schedule is, but my response would be affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there would be any objection from the Prosecution side, I would like to hear that as soon as possible. You don't need to give an immediate answer. You can do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will enquire with Mr. Ierace and we'll inform the Chamber later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We'll then adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please -- Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just in relation to the observation that you made before the break as to the timetable. I don't expect that would be a problem. If I could briefly explain. We were notified by the Defence this morning that there is a change to the order of witnesses after Dr. Kuljic. Instead of a UN witness, the next witness after Dr. Kuljic will now be Professor Dunjic. If we get to Professor Dunjic tomorrow afternoon, we won't be ready to cross-examine him tomorrow afternoon having previously up until this morning expected that he wouldn't be entering the box until late next week. But looking at the estimated times, I think that's most unlikely to happen. It seem that is we will finish Dr. Guskova and Dr. Kuljic, and we're not likely to get beyond or perhaps into examination-in-chief of Dr. Dunjic. So, Mr. President, in summary, should we unexpectedly complete cross-examination of Dr. Dunjic tomorrow afternoon, we will then seek an adjournment before cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that according to the schedule, Professor Dunjic is expected on Monday. The UN member is flying in on Saturday morning. And due to his long trip and fatigue involved in it, we changed the schedule and informed our colleagues that Professor Dunjic would be testifying on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think it's in the interest of the Prosecution as well to be reminded on this. We said that we will have documents that we will provide as soon as possible to the Prosecution. And it's also in their interest to be able to examine these documents, to see them. If we assume that this UN witness will only be able to come on Monday, obviously the Prosecution will be at a disadvantage and Defence counsel really does not wish this to be the case. We need more time for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the Chamber has sometimes some difficulty in following the quick change of the order of appearance of witnesses, we try to cope with it. And I do understand that as such there's no major objection against sitting also for one hour and a half tomorrow in the afternoon. Having read the exchange of correspondence and also having read the -- what the Defence expects from the UN witnesses, I may take it that on the basis of the reciprocal disclosure, that as soon as whatever documents have arrived, that the Defence is under an obligation to provide copies to the Prosecution and not first to inspect them thoroughly and discuss them thoroughly, but right in the beginning to provide copies to the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The problem is that we have noticed that on several occasions -- we intervened on Sunday. We tried to contact someone from this Tribunal. But the door was closed. We weren't able to find out where these people were. This witness will be arriving on Saturday. We could do this on Sunday, but I don't know whether I can bother people at home on a Sunday. So this is a problem of organisation that I don't have under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Ierace, that the Prosecution, apart from what it will say at a later stage and whether these documents have been timely disclosed or not, but the Prosecution might be interested to receive copies as soon as they are available. Since it seems that this witness usually speaks English, they might be in English. I've got no idea. But there's a chance that they are in English. So I take it that the parties will be able to communicate even during the weekend. And if they need any assistance, I'm available because I'm in the Netherlands during the weekend. I'm willing to receive as a post box if necessary or to take care that there is a post box. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. With regard to technical details, this -- well, first of all, I would like to thank you. But perhaps it should be possible for someone to offer us to copy this material. I know that he's going to come with a certain number of cassettes, and I must admit that I don't see how we can copy this -- we don't have machines for copying this. I can do this in Geneva, but it's not the same in The Hague. So I don't know if the Prosecution would like to talk about this later on and see whether we can solve these technical problems for the coming Sunday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that both parties take the necessary measures in order not -- in order not to confront the Chamber next week with all the communication problems that have arisen over the weekend. And copying in Geneva should be the same as copying in The Hague, but we'll see. Perhaps we could now resume the examination of the expert witness, who's waiting already and listened to our procedural issues. Madam Guskova, the Defence will now resume your examination as an expert witness. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when my bookkeeping is correct, then you would have 20 more minutes available. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, given the fact that we don't have much time, I'd be grateful if you could respond very briefly. You mentioned in the course of your testimony a minute ago, you mentioned the name of General Briquemont. Can you tell us very briefly what happened to this general.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: If we're speaking of General Briquemont, he slammed the door and left the mission. Not literally speaking. He did that because he was not -- he did not approve of the methodology of the work of blue helmet forces. He believed that the majority of the adopted UN resolutions were implemented. And in addition to that, he had very serious problems with the safe havens. He believed that resolution 836, 824, which pertained to safe havens or protected areas, were proclaimed on paper only but were not implemented in practice. Instead of 7.000 troops, they were assigned 2.000 troops, and therefore it was impossible to implement those resolutions. In addition, that there were serious disagreements concerning the fact that these protected areas were supposed to become demilitarised zones. And this is something that Briquemont insisted upon. At the same time, in the Security Council there were serious arguments and disagreements concerning the definition of protected areas as areas which could be subjected only to attack by the Serb side. It was not envisioned that they could have been subjected to the attack by the Muslim side. Therefore, in view of General Briquemont's attitude, the Muslim side accused them of being biased and he, following that, left the mission. When other officers arrived at the mission and upon glimpsing what the situation was, all of them became rapidly aware of the fact that the situation was much more difficult than it had seemed at first sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I received the request from the French transcribers that you not put your next question to the witness until the translation in French has been completed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, what can you tell us - but very briefly - about the way the Muslim forces were able to use these zones that you have mentioned? And in particular, I'm referring to Sarajevo. What can you tell us about this in the wartime situation?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: As I've already said, there was a disagreement regarding the fact that these zones were supposed to be demilitarised. However, the sides were unable to reach agreement within the Security Council, and the zones, the areas in the five cities that I've mentioned, were not demilitarised in the end. As a result of that, the Muslim army was able to concentrate its military force within those five cities. We know that the Muslim side did not -- Muslim army did not leave Sarajevo, Tuzla, Srebrenica. And because of that they were able to conduct their military operations in these towns and out of these towns. This is mentioned in the reports of the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this have an effect not only on the continuation of the war but also on its duration; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But what do you mean by that? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: When unfavourable conditions were created for one side and favourable conditions for the troops of the other side, they start using or abusing these conditions, and this is exactly what the Muslim side did. This is a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would like to move on to another subject and to focus on the issue of what we call provocations here. Are you aware of the existence of provocations in the media; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I would call that different. I really appreciate the question that you put to me because we analysed this issue in depth. This was not a provocation by mass media. This is a developed system of provocations which one can observe or see from a historical distance. You can't look at them independently. You have to look at them all together. What is this all about? There are a whole number of cases following which certain actions aimed against certain sides ensued. And simply speaking these are provocations which were aimed at punishing Serbs. Let's analyse the case of preparing sanctions against Yugoslavia on the 30th of May, 1990. Not all of the members of the Security Council were convinced that sanctions were necessary, and therefore something was needed in order to pressure them into agreeing to this. And immediately following that, on the 27th of May an incident took place at Vase Miskina Street. In 1994, NATO revved up its planes to punish Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and an incident was needed in order to bring this into action, following which on the 5th of February, 1994, Markale incident took place. After that there was another incident on Markale, and following that another more intense NATO action against Serbs. Therefore, when analysing this, we came to the conclusion that this was not without intention, and it was intended to punish the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Since we have other questions, I suggest that if I make a gesture, you should take that to mean that you should stop and that we will move on to other subjects. This is just a suggestion. Could you briefly tell us why you can affirm before this Trial Chamber that the so-called Vase Miskina incident represented such a provocation, such a way of attempting to manipulate matters? What are your sources? How do you know this, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, one has to favour logical thinking on one side and comments by General MacKenzie, who in his book said that there had been ballistic experts which -- who pointed out that there were some strange cases and incidents. However, there are no reports concerning this within UN records. I believe that something will appear next year. And if you give me some time, I can point out these peculiarities and weird aspects of these incidents. First of all, there were only Serbs queuing up in the line. The line was not intended to stretch in the street, but they were asked to wait in the street. The street had been blocked earlier and only certain people were let through. And what is most unusual and strange was that there were TV cameras standing ready and Briquemont said -- I'm sorry, MacKenzie said that after the explosion all they needed to do was approach this site, come closer by several metres, and make a footage of what had happened. Several hours later the entire world was informed of what had happened. Serbs had been accused. And after several days the Security Council, influenced by this footage as well, voted in favour of sanctions, although in the report of the Secretary-General it is nowhere mentioned that it was only the Serb side that was guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, without telling us what you were thinking of, for reasons of time, do you think that in the history of Sarajevo there are other situations, other events of a provocative nature that are comparable in terms of their nature and political effects to what you have just mentioned here? Could you just answer by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to another subject now. I would like to talk about another problem, a historical problem. This has to do with the meeting between Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and the American ambassador at the time, Mr. Zimmerman. In your report you make certain claims with regard to what happened immediately after the meeting, that is to say, with regard to Mr. Izetbegovic's change of heart, the fact that he changed his position. What do you know about this? How do you know about this? Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, you're referring to Cutilheiro's plan. Am I right? The meeting between Zimmerman and Alija Izetbegovic is described in detail in Zimmerman's book. He doesn't say what advice he gave to Izetbegovic, and Izetbegovic in his own book also fails to mention that he had received an advice from Zimmerman, although people who were close to them said to me that there had been a particular advice. Nobody denies the fact that there had been a meeting, and the meeting took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I assume that it was somewhere in the area of Sarajevo. However, Zimmerman says that immediately following the meeting with Alija Izetbegovic, he returned to Belgrade and sent a wire to his superiors in the United States saying that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be recognised immediately. Logically analysing this, we can conclude that after this conversation Alija Izetbegovic refused to sign the Cutilheiro plan and all of the efforts of the United States were directed at recognising Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another subject now. I would like to talk about the persecution of Serbs in Sarajevo. In your report you mentioned that this -- such persecution had to do with the salaries Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 19447 to 19457. which depended on ethnic membership. And you also mentioned a point that I am interested in now, and that has to do with the massacre of the Kazani graves. I would like you to tell us what sources you used and what information you had at your disposal with regard to the number of possible victims in these graves.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Concerning the victims in Sarajevo, a number of documents and records are emerging. In 1992, 1993, and 1994, during the conflict there was practically no information. The information is emerging now. And in 1994, a trial was instigated against Muslim soldiers who had committed crimes in Kazani. There were 14 people involved who committed crimes, and this was reported in the papers. People are expecting that more information will emerge regarding this crime, and there are different numbers that are circulated, although it is widely believed that between two and seven thousand people were killed there, in that incident. In some different reports, it is mentioned that the number of victims went as high as 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the French booth, it's not 200 but perhaps 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, were you yourself in Sarajevo? Were you able to see how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're correcting the translation. I'd always rather have this confirmed by the witness. It's not up to one of the parties to say that. But is it correct that you said two to seven thousand, rather than two to seven hundred, as the first figures you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two to seven thousand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, were you yourself in Sarajevo during the period that we are interested in, 1992-1994? And if so, can you describe the daily life that you were able to observe there. Not just that of soldiers but also the daily life led by the civilians. What sort of impressions could an observer gain?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. This is going outside the area of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague should read pages -- read through pages 61, 62, and 63 or should reread these pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The personal impressions of the expert witness while visiting Sarajevo is part of the report, as I remember. So in this respect, I would say the expert witness is also a bit a witness of fact in this respect. Or would you have any objection against that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you understood my question, madam?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, I've understood the question, and I'll try to answer it briefly. I was in Sarajevo in September 1994 after a long interval, because before that I was in Sarajevo in the 1970s. And I read a great deal about destruction, about exchanges of fire. And to be quite honest, as a historian what struck me was that Gavrilo Princip's museum was gone and the library was gone. As a scientist it was very hard to see that. But following the bank of the Miljacka, I didn't see any major destructions. I did see that in Vase Miskina all the kiosks were back up. And I still remember a domestic scene how a Muslim vendor is carrying coffee to his neighbour. So it was a rather peaceful scene. In other words, Bascarsija, that was the heart of the city, was operating. There was only one important building that was seriously damaged. And that was the building -- the photograph of which appeared in all the newspapers and everywhere, and that was not far from the hotel -- the hotel in which all the journalists and international mediators lived. But otherwise, the city lived. We were of course advised not to walk around the city, but I wanted to see it so I did walk. But I did walk around -- I wanted to see what it was like, and I felt safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask for one clarification. You said there was only one important building that was seriously damaged and that was next to a hotel where the international journalists were residing. What -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the building that was seriously damaged you were referred to? You said there was only one. Which one did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The adminstrati. It was a government building. It was a high-rise building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You also spoke about the museum of Gavrilo Princip. Could you tell us who, according to you, destroyed that museum.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Well, in an event which took place near Gavrilo Princip's museum is a plate -- is an iron plate in the place where he stood when he fired at the -- at the arch-duke. This iron plate -- this metal plate was simply taken out, pulled out of the pavement. And as far as I know, this museum was not destroyed. It was simply looted. It was completely plundered, and it no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your 20 minutes are over approximately, so if you could conclude in a couple of -- two or three minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, and very quickly, please, with regard to Markale and a possible problem, a matter of provocation, what could you tell us in a minute?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Very briefly, I do not doubt at all that the shelling of Markale did not happen from the Serb side, and there is evidence to corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us regarding the investigation that was conducted, if you, that is, know something about that?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: As early as 1996, Yasushi Akashi in his interview to a German paper said that there was a document about the UN investigations showing that it was not done by the Serb side. David Owen speaks about that -- writes about that in his book and does it very eloquently. If there were enough time, I'd quote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You say -- you say in your report that David Owen said that his information could not be revealed -- or who said that the United Nations decided that such information should not be revealed, should not be disclosed? So how do you know these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interpreter speak up, please. David Owen writes in his book that there were four reasons for which this information should not be disclosed. One of the reasons is that NATO troops were already ready to strike positions and that changed plans completely. The second reason, where possible refusal of Alija Izetbegovic to take part in further negotiations, which was very important. The third reason was that everybody was already convinced, that is, everybody was quite sure that allegedly this shell had come from the Serb side and that completely changed the picture of what had happened. And one of the principal reasons was that it could have prejudiced the authority of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only two questions more, Mr. President, the last and the one before the last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So my penultimate question, and very briefly: Madam, does -- when the so-called Muslim forces were formed, the Green Berets and then the Patriotic League, the formation of these forces, was this indicative of the wish to wage war rather than a wish to have peace? Or what -- how would you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Well, in one sentence, it would be -- my answer would be this: The formation of a Muslim armed formations beginning in April 1991, when the negotiations concerning the future of the SFRY was still underway, testifies to the intentions to fight for the independence of Bosnia with arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you. This is the answer you gave in your report, isn't it? You're reflecting now what is in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was answering questions. I don't remember. I was answering questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you will have a question which has not been, as the last three questions, finds an answer in the report. The Bench, of course, has read the report very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My very last question, Mr. President, is as follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, can you confirm to us under oath the integrity of your report which we have all read carefully, or would you -- and/or would you like to add something to it? This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I can add a great deal to my report because of late a large number of documents have emerged which could supplement or complement what I've written in it. But the concept as such, no, I wouldn't change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it then -- because the last question were two questions, as a matter of fact. First, whether you confirm whatever is in your report. I do understand that you answered that question in the affirmative and that you would like to add a lot. But perhaps that question should have been put a bit earlier to you rather than as the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Guskova.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could the interpreters speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or come closer to the microphone. The witness has some difficulties in hearing the -- perhaps the volume could be adjusted so that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
