utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, yes. Of course. Yes. That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I take you to page 52 of your report, where you reported on the Markale incident. Perhaps the corresponding page -- I have the English translation. You begin that section with the words, "In the Sarajevo marketplace Markale, on February 5th, 1994, at 12.20 hours, a strong explosion happened with unknown provenance of fired shells." And you use the term "shells," in the plural. Is it your position that several shells had been fired in the course of the Markale explosion of February 5th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Different sources say that there were between one and three shells, and that is why I put it as you see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you yourself have not arrived at a particular conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I wasn't at the Markale market, and all the information that I had come from literature, when the authors said what the -- I took it from the authors who mentioned one, two, or three projectiles, and that is why I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You report further that eight persons were killed in the incident. What is the source of your information to conclude that only eight persons were killed?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I think this is a misprint. The text should have said "68."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sixty-eight, you say. Yes. Because on the next page you're talking about -- you quote, at least, 80 persons killed. So that's -- but, therefore, I understood "8" to be a misprint. But I thought of 80, but now you've explained to us that you have 68 in your mind. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, do you know of the UNPROFOR investigation that was conducted by way of a special team of experts into the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: If you are referring to the Markale market I, to begin with it was discussed at the blue helmet headquarters while I was there and later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. If I may interrupt you. I'm referring to the Markale market explosion of the 5th February, 1994, which is what the section in your report refers to. And my question to you is whether you know of the UNPROFOR investigation which was conducted into the incident. Do you know that such an investigation was conducted whereby a special team of experts investigated into the incident and reported on it?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I'm saying that there was an investigation and there were the first conclusion and the second one which was sent to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you read the UNPROFOR investigation report which has been published?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: This investigation is mentioned in the report of the Secretary-General to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, in your report you do not refer to the findings of the UNPROFOR investigation team into the incident. So I'm asking you, have you read the report?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: No, I did not read the report myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown P2261A.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I take it, madam, that you read English. The quote is in English.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is a question that you have not read this report before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it perhaps please be put on the ELMO for just one second, since there are so many reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar has just drawn my attention to the fact that although the document has an R number, that it's not tendered and admitted under seal. So I take it that it can be put on the ELMO, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please put it on the ELMO. It's a bit inconvenient for you, but putting it on this machine allows us to read together with you. So if you would please turn to the -- either read from the screen or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really see it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could also turn to the original, which is to the left of you on that machine. The usher would certainly assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, at the outset you testified that in arriving at your conclusions you approached the subject in an extremely scientific manner.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Therefore, prior to reporting on the Markale market incident of February 5th, 1994, should you not have perused the UNPROFOR investigation report in order for your opinion to be an objective and impartial one?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm putting it to you. Should you not have first read this report prior to compiling your section on the Markale market explosion in order for your report to be an impartial and objective report?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact I do not think that this report would have changed my opinion, because the main reason for which this incident happened, they're quite sure that it was a set-up, and it worked. So that is why such an opinion emerged. Another thing is important, that there are, in writing, the opinions of people who were near the place of incident and which refute the official point of view, and that allows us to question it and to try to follow a different line of reasoning, precisely in an attempt to be more objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, would you please turn to page 3 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps the document may be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You will see quite contrary to what you report the investigation team has found that the explosion was in fact caused by 120-millimetre high explosive mortar and also, quite contrary to what you asserted with regard to the casualties being inconsistent with a mortar bomb explosion, the investigation team has found the casualties to be consistent with a mortar bomb explosion. In view of this report, the official findings of the UNPROFOR team of investigators, on what information or on what basis do you conclude otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: In this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we have first the image corrected. If we are to follow the debate, we really need to see the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please stay with it, Mr. Usher, so that we -- So your question was on the basis of what you have drawn a conclusion different from the one on this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you what line of logic did I follow in coming to my conclusions. To begin with, I took this official point of view which I heard and which indeed existed at that time in 1994, and say this is the -- these are the thoughts of the officers that I talked to at the time in 1994. The subject of our conversation was the reason which NATO found to develop its activities in that territory. And what I believe, that our conclusions were then confirmed by later findings. For instance, in what Lord Owen writes later in his book, and he said that there was a document and there is the opinion of one ballistics expert who believed that that shell could not have arrived from the Serb side, because it either exploded directly there on the market or came from somewhere else. On the other hand, in the conversation with Colonel Demurenko, who in relation to the incident Markale II, and he was talking to me as a ballistics expert. Unfortunately, I am not an expert on ballistics, so I can only convey to you his opinion. And he said that there was no such 120-millimetre shell which could produce such a large number of casualties. And thirdly, the thing which made me start questioning all this was Mr. Yasushi Akashi's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for clarification first. On page 53 of your report you are referring to a conversation with Mr. Demurenko in which it reads, "I have in mind 12-millimetre mine," whereas you just, as far as I understood you correctly, you said "120" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be 120. 120. Yes, a typing error again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make things absolutely clear, I speak as a principal, but nevertheless the name of Demurenko which you mentioned is -- which we read in that text, is it the same name that the witness mention a moment ago? Because we do not see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's been mentioned many times before. I don't think there was any confusion in that respect. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, you stated that the report would not have changed your mind. Even if you had read the report, it would not have changed your mind. As an expert, isn't it incumbent upon you to examine all material relevant to a particular issue, especially an impartial investigation which has been conducted into the incident, the report relating to it, prior to issuing an opinion on it?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: You are quite right. But I never denied that there was an official view concerning the explosion at Markale I that you are talking about. What I tried to do was introduce a doubt, that is, to point out that there was a different view other than the official one, and that one is the one that I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is: Even knowing that there was an official investigation, you did not take the time to peruse the official investigation report but based your conclusions on discussions with other people, the sources of which you really do not refer to in your report?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Experience shows us that unless you question a document, unless you check a document, then you can never attain the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to another area. I draw your attention to page 21 of your report.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Could you please give me the heading so that I can find it quickly in the Russian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's a section entitled "War objectives." And I'm referring to the second paragraph under the section, which refers to the war objectives of the Serb side. Now, you enumerate four Bosnian Serb objectives under the title "War objectives." Are you aware of the six strategic goals adopted by the Bosnian Serb Assembly at its 16th session in Banja Luka on 12th May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you also aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make. We have to focus on what took place in Sarajevo. And I think that trying to retrace the course of history in Banja Luka is not really necessary at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you wanted to have to focus exclusively on Sarajevo, you should have presented a different report. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, are you also aware that those six strategic objectives were reiterated at a meeting of the presidents of the municipalities on 14th May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Six strategic goals that you are mentioning are completely different things from these objectives. In my report, I mentioned the objectives of the Serbs in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had to do with their future. Whereas, the six so-called strategic goals that you are mentioning are not really a strategy but, rather, a tactic. Therefore, they could be considered as sub-items or ways of implementing objectives of the leadership of Republika Srpska. So these are two completely different matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, would you be able to identify those six objectives if you were shown a document listing them?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: No, I am aware of these six strategic goals. The first one --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. I asked you the question whether you were aware that those six strategic objectives were reiterated at a meeting of the presidents of the municipalities on 14 May 1992, two days after they were adopted at the assembly sessions. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that they were not adopted but, rather, debated on, and certain people were informed about them. Therefore, I believe that using the word "adopted" is not appropriate. The document was drafted and all of the Serb municipalities had to be informed of it, but it was not adopted. So shall I enumerate the strategic goals for you now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit P3413. It's a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, would you please read out the title of this document or identify this document.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: "Meeting with presidents of municipalities in the area of responsibility of the division." A meeting with presidents of municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the division.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On page 2 you will find the six strategic objectives which were just referred to. Do you identify them? Page 2.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the agenda of this document where --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, please. My question to you is whether you could identify the six strategic objectives which are enumerated on page 2. Do you see those six objectives set out on page 2?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, would you please refer to the fifth objective. Could you read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: In Russian it would sound as follows: "It was said that Sarajevo had to be either divided or levelled to the ground."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you called this, to use your own terms, "tactics," and not "objectives," as you've enumerated on page 21. Now, how does this relate to the four objectives you set out in page 21? Which objective -- which Serbian objective that you enumerated in page 21 encompasses this particular tactic, that is, the fifth tactic, Sarajevo should be divided or levelled to the ground?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Allow me to respond, please. The document that you're showing to me is not the document that was adopted at the session on the 12th of May, 1992. The Assembly of Serb Peoples adopted six strategic goals which have a completely different character and consequences. The first goal was to divide the state from two other national entities. Then in goal 2, 3, and 4 they spoke about uniting those areas, extending the corridor in the area of Brcko, in the valley of the rivers Drina and Una. And then the fifth item, if you look carefully at the records of the meeting, they spoke about splitting Sarajevo into a Serbian and a Muslim side. In Karadzic's report, it was said that the Serbian state could not exist without Sarajevo as well as that Alija's state could not exist without Sarajevo. The sixth goal spoke about access to the sea. And the document that you are showing to me is a document from a meeting - at least that's how it looks to me - but it seems that the person who signed this document attended the assembly session and then came back to his or her municipality and then reported to them about what had transpired at the session. Therefore, we cannot take this to be the strategic goal that was presented at the session on the 12th of May and was recorded as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you referred to in your report as your fourth objective to conclude a cease-fire on all the battlefronts and reinforce Serb positions in the entire territory of Republika Srpska. Now, which tactic or strategic objective enumerated in that document would relate to the fourth objective?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to? Could you please repeat that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document before you, which is placed before you. My question -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: This one here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see any relationship to the fourth objective enumerated by you and the six strategic objectives or tactics, as you put it, set out in this document?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Generally these goals correspond to those that had been adopted at the session of the assembly. The first one, the second one, the third one, the fourth one, and the sixth one. All but the phrase concerning Sarajevo levelled to the ground. There was no such phrase mentioned in the document from the assembly. So it could have been an emotional conveying of what had transpired at the assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, who has presided this meeting? I'm referring to the meeting this document relates to. Could you please examine the document and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could we first ask whether the witness has seen this document before. And could we ask her whether she has been present. I mean, reading in a document who is presiding a meeting, that is something apart from that -- it has been extensively dealt with in previous testimonies -- might not be something you should ask from an expert witness. I mean, the only thing you ask her is whether she can read or not. The Chamber will accept that she can read.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless you have any specific reason to ask this specific witness. But you may -- if it's of any use, then of course you may draw her attention to the fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, isn't it the case that the second, fourth, and since you challenged the fifth objective I will not refer it to -- and the sixth -- the second, fourth, and sixth goals which you do concede to enumerated in this document are not encompassed in the four objectives that you reported on in your -- in page 21 of your report?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I will continue insisting upon the terminology. When we're speaking about what the Serb people were fighting for, that's one thing. We can call it "goals of the Serb peoples fighting." And if we're talking about the means they would use to implement that and what they specifically mean under that, then that could be called "a tactic." I can also formulate this question in a different way. I've already spoken about that when I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you the following: Would you please carefully listen to the questions put to you and answer to those questions. I think what Ms. Mahindaratne asked you: "and I think it relates to your testimony where you said that the six strategic goals, or rather, tactics, and could be considered as sub-items or ways of implementing objectives of the leadership of Republika Srpska." Ms. Mahindaratne now ask you to explain to her whether these six, as you call them, "tactics," where they can be related to the four objectives you described in your report on page 21. Because you explained to us before that these were more or less sub-items. She specifically asked you whether these were sub-items, apart from the discussion on whether number 5 really reflects what were the tactics, but how you can relate these tactical six points to, she specifically asked, number 4 of your war objectives, and if it could be categorised under number 3, 2, or 1, please tell us. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we exclude the ending phrase of item 5, then we could say that they fully correspond to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But how are they related - that was the question - to either number 4 or any of the other war objectives you described in your report? Because you explained to us that these were sub-items of the war objectives you described. So the question now is: How to relate these six -- six, as you told us, tactical goals to the war objectives you described. That is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relation is very simple. When we say that certain area needs to be kept under control, the area mostly populated by Serbian people, then that means that that territory needs to be compact and must be linked by certain corridors. Items 1, 2, and 3 speak about the corridors that had to link these territories. Item which speaks about the River Drina fully corresponds to item 3 in my report. As far as concluding a truce, that is a particular tactic of the Army of Republika Srpska which they used throughout the entire period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] May I draw your attention to page 39 of your report.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Could you please give me the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I would like to know, on page 2 of the translation of this document -- because you are not going to use this document any more, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will come back to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know if it says -- line 13 or something like that. Page 2 of the original is missing. Do you have page 2 of the original? Because I think that we have this document. We received this document before, but I am not sure. I think that we did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to page 2 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- Of the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 is missing in my copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Page 2 -- I am asking -- I am asking to the Prosecutor's counsel. My question is whether you have the -- page 2 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is how it has been translated, Your Honour: In fact, page 2 of the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Page 2 is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is the way we've received the document, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In page 39, as I said --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: What heading, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You referred to -- the title is "Situation around Sarajevo." And I draw your attention to the last paragraph, where you refer to nine municipalities and you claim that these municipalities were populated mostly with Serb population. Now, for which period are you referring to here when you say that these municipalities were populated by -- mostly by Serb population? Are you referring to the period prior to the outbreak of the conflict or thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me in greater detail what paragraphs you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the paragraph where you start off with "Leadership of the Republika Srpska wished at any cost to keep Sarajevo as its capital or at least part of the city. Sarajevo with its suburbs is a very large city, nine municipalities covered 1.113 kilometre square populated mostly with Serb population, were controlled by Serbs and were within the composition of the Republika Srpska." And you name the nine municipalities. That's the paragraph I'm referring to. It is the second paragraph under the section "Situation around Sarajevo." Have you --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now -- well, my question to you is: For which period are you referring to when you say these nine municipalities were mostly populated by Serb population?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I was referring to the time period when Sarajevo had already been divided along the ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give in terms of -- was it prior to the conflict, in the course of the conflict, after the conflict? Can you give in terms of years?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: That was after the division of Sarajevo along the ethnic lines, because the majority of Serb residents from ten municipalities were only in four of them. But the borders had already been changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... What was the source of your information? Could you give the year, if it was based on a census or -- what period are you referring to here? Is that a difficult question to answer?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: No, it's not a difficult question for me. I simply want to clarify it. I was not referring to municipalities -- to ten municipalities which according to the census covered Sarajevo. I was here referring to other territories, including the municipalities which were encompassed by Serbian Sarajevo after 1992, or let's say in the second part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... You have clearly stated in this last paragraph - and I quote to you - "leadership of Republika Srpska wished at any cost to keep Sarajevo as its capital or at least part of the city. Sarajevo with its suburbs is a very large city. Nine municipalities, populated mostly with Serb population were controlled by Serbs and were within the composition of Republika Srpska." And then you go on to name, they were the following municipalities. Now, why -- what is it that you're referring to when you say you were not referring to municipalities? Clearly when you said that nine municipalities were mostly populated by Serb population you're referring to these nine municipalities. My question to you is: What is the source of your information? Why are you reluctant to answer this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to avoid confusion, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I approach this in a different way, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just ask you the following: In page 39 you are referring to nine municipalities populated mostly with Serb population. Did I understand your testimony correctly that you were referring to the situation in -- after 1992 or at least in the second part of 1992, not to the period prior to the outbreak of an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you referred to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to that, it is emphasised here that I was referring to the Serbian population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were referring to the statistics of the Serb authorities. Your report reads, "In these parts of the city which was called Serb Sarajevo, according to the statistics of the Serb authorities, 120.000 persons were living." Do you have the date of these statistics? And perhaps I should look in footnote 276 because that's what the testimony, as far as I understand, says and that's what the report says, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. This pertains to the personal -- to the information on Sarajevo printed in newspaper Oslobodjenje in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So would it be then correct to say that the -- these statistics are for 1995? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: They were published in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of these nine municipalities prior to the outbreak of the war? Was it still a case of majority of Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: The Serbs were a majority only in four municipalities. In Pale they constituted 68 per cent of the population; Ilijas, Ilidza, and Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown a document, Mr. President. It's the population census, the large document. Therefore, it may be placed on the ELMO. I don't have sufficient copies to pass around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- if you'd like to show that to the witness, you're fully entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be put on the ELMO in such a way that we can follow it clearly on the screen. Could you indicate what page you would like to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: First of all, madam, do you recognise the census which has been shown to you? Have you gone through this before?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: You know what? When it comes to geographic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... If I may interrupt you. My question to you was whether you perused this census before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, simply we know that there were at least three censuses in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'd like to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Which census are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... And I think that it is on the ELMO. And if you would look at your screen, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would have no great difficulties to find out what date -- what year, at least, is mentioned in the document. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne. But may I ask you: If there's any further comments you would like to make, ask me whether you can comment. But first answer the questions. If there's anything important to be added, please tell me and I will give you an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I was wondering whether this would be an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be an appropriate time. We will adjourn until ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher -- oh, yes. I see that the witness is being brought in. Ms. Mahindaratne, the Chamber wonders why you tell us that page 2 of a document is not available if the Chamber could find it in five minutes during the break. Would it not have been appropriate for the Prosecution to provide a full copy of that document? I'm going to refer you to annex 83 to the report of Dr. Donia, exactly the same document, although under a different ERN number. But the Chamber feels no -- that it's not responsible for double filing of same documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President. I was under the impression that it was not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, may I just verify how long I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I have to -- I did a search rather than the bookkeeping at this moment. But I think you started, Ms. Mahindaratne, at 5.00. Then we went on to ten minutes to 6.00. It is approximately 50 minutes you've used by now. And since the Defence took a little bit over one hour and a half, then you know that some 40, 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence also spent some time finding page 2. We'd like to know -- because it seems -- it seemed that it was a new document, but we all now know that it was not a new document. Could we know what the translation was based on. I am talking about page 2, which was, we believe, deliberately dropped out, we think. We believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's certainly not the case, Mr. President. Sometimes there are several translations made with regard to one particular document, and I believe what happened was that one of those translations which did not have the -- have page 2 was tendered with the B/C/S, the original. And it is my fault, but certainly there was no ulterior motives attached to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any specific reason why the Defence takes it that on purpose page 2 was left out whereas it was already in evidence? If there's no specific reason ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Because -- because no questions were asked -- no questions were asked of this witness about what was this, the comment as such. And I will need more time to ask questions in my re-examination. And we think that if the witness had this whole document, that perhaps the answers would have been different. And that is why we think that this was done on purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not fully convinced yet, but we'll deliberate in the Chamber whether there's any reason to believe that there was any intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend too much time on it. We have now -- at least you have a -- there is a full copy available if anyone would like to inspect it either in translation or not, I have it with me at this very moment. If not, let's please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I have a copy of that or might I borrow your copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, please refer to page 7 of the official census. I'm referring to the page which starts with Sarajevo and then Centar. Now, you list Centar as one of the municipalities which had a majority Serbian population, on page 39 of your report. The total population in Centar is 79.286, according to this census. And the Muslim population is 39.761. The Serbian population, 16.631; Croatian, 5.428; Yugoslavian, 13.030; and others, 4.436. Below that there is Hadzici, another municipality that you've listed as having a majority Serbian population. The total population, according to this census, is 24.200; Muslim population, 15.392; Serbian, 6.362; Croatian, 746; Yugoslavian, 841; and others, 859. And I also take you to page 8, which lists Ilidza, total population 67.937; Muslim population is 29.337; Serbian 25.029; Croatian, 6.934; Yugoslavian, 5.181; and others, 1.456. Likewise, you would see below that Ilijas. Total, 25.184, on the same page; Muslim, 10.585, Serbian, 11.325; Croatian, 1.736; Yugoslavian, 1.167; and others, 371. And I draw your attention to page number 10, to Novi Grad, which is also a municipality you've listed as having a majority Serbian population. The total is 136.616, out of which Muslim population is 69.430; Serbian, 37.591; Croatian, 8.889; Yugoslavian, 15.580; and others, 5.126. Below that, Novo Sarajevo -- I beg your pardon. You have not listed Novi Grad but Novo Sarajevo, which gives the total population of 95.089; Muslim population, 33.902; Serbian, 32.899; Croatian, 8.798; Yugoslavian, 15.099; others, 4.391. I draw your attention to page 12, which lists Stari Grad and Trnovo, which are two municipalities listed by you. Total, 50.744; Muslim population, 39.410; Serbian population, 5.150; Croatian, 1.126; Yugoslavian, 3.374; and others, 1.684. Trnovo, likewise, total 6.991; Muslim population, 4.790; Serb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the text on the ELMO be moved, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please move the text on the ELMO such that the interpreters could -- perhaps not zoom out, because it might even be more difficult, but to move a little bit upwards and then zoom in again. That's downwards. If the document would be moved upwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in Trnovo the Serbian population is 2.059; Croatian, 16; Yugoslavia, 72; and others, 54. And finally, on page 13, Vogosca. Total, 24.647; Muslim population, 12.499; Serbian, 8.813; Croatian, 1.071; Yugoslavian, 1.730; and others, 534. So according to this census, which is indicated as a final census of 1991, except for Ilijas, all other municipalities -- all the other municipalities that you listed as having a majority of Serb population in 1991, according to your source reference, had a majority of Muslim population prior to the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So do you agree, then, that prior to the conflict in these municipalities there were mostly Muslim population living, whereas after the war, if your source citation is to be depended on, there -- those municipalities had acquired a majority of Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I'd like to make something clear with regard to my text. I'm not talking about the ten municipalities listed in the census of 1991. I am referring to territories and parts of municipalities and their boundaries did not correspond to the boundaries of the former municipalities. We are talking about the Republika Srpska, which was made of municipalities with a mixed population according to the 1991 census. But it is better to rely on the census of 1981, which is also official. I fully agree in six municipalities out of ten, the Muslims were the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to another area. In page --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the document be returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In page 45, if I may draw your attention to page 45 of the document -- of your report.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Which chapter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Under the chapter "Suffering of Serbs," two pages down. You start off -- this is on page 45, paragraph 1. You start off with, "The city was blocked from the outside but it was blocked much more from the inside, and this blockade was experienced as a much harder one." And then further down that page you refer to these two types of blockades again in a statement attributable to David Owen, and you go on to say, "Sarajevo is actually under a double blockade. The first one was placed by Serbs shelling the city from artillery, armament, and sniper rifles, and by placing a circle around the city. The second blockade was made by the army of the Bosnian government which had restricted its people by interior blockade and bureaucratic obstacles." Now, in the first paragraph, when you referred to the city being blocked from the outside, you were referring to -- were you not referring to the first one, what David Owen is speaking about, the first one is placed by Serbs shelling the city from artillery, armament, and sniper rifles, and by placing a circle around the city? That's the outside blockade you are referring to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I didn't really get your question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you found the particular paragraph I'm referring to where you speak of two types of blockades, one from the outside and one from the inside? And you go on to say, "The interior blockade was experienced as a much harder one." Did you find that passage?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Further down in that page you refer to the two types of blockades again in a statement attributable to by David Owen. The first one is described as, "Shelling the city --" let me quote you. "The first one was placed by Serbs shelling the city from artillery, armament, and sniper rifles and by placing a circle around the city." My question to you is: You were referring to this first type of blockade when you referred to an outside blockade to Sarajevo; wasn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: This is not me speaking. It is David Owen. And I am quoting him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is so. But in paragraph 1, you do refer to the two types of blockades. And my question to you is: Presumably you're referring to that -- the first blockade that David Owen is speaking about, that is, the encirclement of Sarajevo and shelling with armament and sniper rifles. That's what you --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes. It was all there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In view of that, what was the basis on which you concluded that the interior blockade, to use your own words, "but it was blocked much more from the inside and the blockade -- and this blockade was experienced as a much harder one." What was the basis for your conclusion that the inside blockade was experienced as a much harder one, as opposed to the outside one and admittedly encirclement of Sarajevo and shelling and firing with sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Regrettably in 1993 and 1994, one could practically not leave the city. That is, people who lived in Sarajevo wanted to leave it. And this also applies to other towns. And the leadership of Republika Srpska repeatedly proposed to the Muslim side to reach an agreement whereby everybody who wanted so could leave the city. And how difficult it was to leave the city, well, I knew that because I worked with UNPROFOR and talked to many people. Today it is written a great deal about those people who participated as blue helmets in Sarajevo, profited from that situation, and for a certain amount of money took people out of Sarajevo, because otherwise it was very difficult. Today, information emerges how these things were happening in Sarajevo. There are documents attesting to this. There are memoirs. There are diaries. I talked with people who had left Sarajevo and who found it very difficult to get out of it. But that was, in point of fact, a government policy. It wasn't the policy pursued by individual municipality leaders or some lower tiers of power. And my observations fully coincide with what I wrote and what you can read in what General Morillon and David Owen also stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to another area. If I may draw your attention to page 48 to 52 of your report where you discuss the imposition of sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is under the title "The use of provocations for purpose of punishing Serbs." On page 49, referring to the report of the Secretary-General, UN Secretary-General, bearing number S-24049, you go on to say this: "In its entirety, the report was presented an extremely complex and diversified situation. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, I did not end with the conclusion that it was necessary to introduce sanctions against Yugoslavia. It seems that this was actually the reason why the report of the UN Secretary-General was allegedly lost somewhere in the offices of the United Nations and that it reached the desks of the Security Council members only after they --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And reached the desks of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you are asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "And it reached the desks of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that since the B/C/S interpretation asked my attention, that there's something wrong now with the channels. On channel 4 I now heard B/C/S translation, where I would expect to hear the original English or English translation. Let's try it again. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "And it reached the desks of the Security Council members only after they had voted on the introduction of sanctions." Now, in making that statement, you're clearly implying that the report of the Secretary-General was prepared after the resolution imposing sanctions was adopted. That's your assertion?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. The report was prepared for that particular session. But it did not turn up on the desks in front of the Security Council members.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct. But in saying that it did not reach the desks of the Security Council members until the resolution was adopted, you obviously imply that the report had not been -- had been already written prior to the resolution was adopted -- that the report was prepared before the adoption of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was the source of your information that this report got lost in the United Nations and did not reach the desks until the adoption of the resolution?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Many media outlets wrote about that. In June of 1994 there were hearings held in the parliament of the Russian Federation concerning this issue and I, as an expert of the parliament, had in my possession all documents relating to the imposition of sanctions and the attitude of Russia concerning that. And at the time we were discussing the issue regarding why Russia had put its signature on the document imposing sanctions. So this was based on the documents in our possession at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam, prior to making that assertion, did you take the time to peruse the whole report in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown a document. It's the report of the Secretary-General bearing number S-24049 of 30th May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, madam, your position was that this report was prepared prior to the resolution was adopted, that is, resolution 757. That's your position. Would you please read the final paragraph of the report, that is, paragraph number 17. Is it clear to you that by this paragraph that this report has been prepared only after the resolution had been adopted? Because there is a reference to the Security Council's decision today to impose sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There's a reference to the resolution. So is it clear to you now that your position that this report was prepared prior to the adoption of the resolution was completely incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Based on the fact that the report itself appeared later, it is quite possible that it was written up later on. When we analysed this at our parliament session, this paragraph was missing. It wasn't there. We had it in a different draft.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the United Nations Secretary-General has added a paragraph to this document later on to mislead some party? Is that what your -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I don't know how this came about. I have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But are you implying that this document has been altered?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I wish to say that the report of the Secretary-General was written based on the information of his representatives and it was prepared specifically for the 30th and this session that took place on that day, the session of the Security Council. And based on the report of the report, they voted and adopted a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to put these questions, could the Prosecution now decide with regard to this second page, the translation, could it decide which document we're going to be working on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Phantom page. As far as I understand, there is a document that has been used to be translated, a document without page 2, and therefore the translation incorrectly says that page 2 is missing, I take it that the translators have been presented a document with a missing page 2. And we had already in evidence an annex to the report of Dr. Donia, a report -- a document which seems to be exactly the same do you mean, including stamps, et cetera, which contains a second page. So I -- and of course we were confronted only recently, but I'm certain that if you would like to have the -- either the original with the page 2 that is already known to you, but if you would like to look at it again, I'll be glad to provide you with the B/C/S copy. And perhaps Mr. Ierace has finished by now the English translation so that you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And during the break and shortly after you alerted us to this, as a result of some inquiries made during the break we have located the full copy together with the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you would like to have a look at it, I will be glad to leave both copies with you and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you may now re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have found this document during the break. It's the one that we -- it's the same one that we had. But I wanted to be certain that the Prosecution had the time to do what it should have done before, that is to say, to read this second page. If this is the case, I will proceed with my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you were shown a document before that was not complete. I would now like to have a look at the copy which should have been shown to you, the complete copy which includes page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should I do, Mr. President? Should I provide this document that you have just given me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to ask questions about the document, I think you, with the consent of the parties, would then use this document that has been annex 83 to the report of Dr. Donia. And if there would be a copy available in English for me again, being the only one who provided the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less -- less --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English translation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, could you please briefly read page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like you to read this so that we can translate this as best as possible. The first point 3 on the first page. Could you go back to page number 1, please. The first page -- no, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the booth, it's the first page. It's not the third page. It's the third item, the third point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The first third point, do you see it? It starts with -- could you read the first word out, please.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: "Messages."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Having said that, could you examine this in relation to page 2. That is to say, could this item be applied to what we can see on page 2, that is to say - and I'll have to summarise this - can it be applied to what is taking place in the theatre of operations, with regard to the places, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to waste a little time, Mr. President, but ...

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: It seems to me that this has to do with a meeting at which purely military issues were discussed and also information on what had passed at the Serbian assembly meeting in Banja Luka was presented as well. This is as far as I can gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Hence the character -- the tactical definition that you used. I think that's the term that you employed a while ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you read what we didn't have a look at earlier on. Could you read out loudly - it's the last page of the document. And I have to find it myself -

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've found the place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you read out -- you can do it. You can use the Serbian text which you are familiar with. It's page 4, and it starts with the words "at the end of the meeting," et cetera. Could you read out the part that starts with those words. Could you do that, please.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: "At the end of the meeting, Colonel Galic proposed the following conclusions: Implement the decisions from the meeting in Banja Luka, but it was necessary to submit them to the commands of units and municipalities; hold the present positions and defend them without war; continue with the growth and seek weapons and equipment for new" and then I can see what does this pertain to. "All forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina should work towards the same goals. War profiteering should be prevented. Wartime functioning of the economy should be ensured and neighbouring municipalities should help each other out. All the fighters should be commended for the combat results achieved so far." This is a bad copy. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's quite right. I'll stop you there. It's a bad copy, but thank you very much for having complied with my request. Witness, my question is as follows: Isn't there contradiction, an intrinsic contradiction in this document in that it's hard to explain why it would be necessary to raze Sarajevo to the ground, according to the phrase "[B/C/S spoken]", and at the same time to carry out a defence without engaging in war? Have you understood the question? Because I can see that for the Russian booth --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes, I have understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you going to answer?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I understood the question because the last phrases speak about a meeting that had been held and at which issues that had to do with the results of the assembly session held on the 12th of May in Banja Luka were analysed. The last sentence says that documents from the assembly were analysed and taken into account and not personal -- personal information presented as to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Isn't there contradiction between the term "[B/C/S spoken]" Which I mentioned a minute ago and these indications made by Colonel -- by General Galic that defence should be mounted without engaging in war? Aren't these two positions contradictory in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness is being led. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're seeking -- well, if it's intrinsic, if it comes from the text, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would say it hardly needs any explanation, any confirmation. If it's not intrinsic, you should put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As a result, I would like to move on to another subject. Witness - and I would like to focus on what was pointed out to you. It's at page 48 and 50, and it has to do with reports from UN experts concerning the Markale incident. Could you answer my question by saying yes or no. Are you a ballistics expert; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question already. She said, "I'm not a ballistics expert," so there's no reason to ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right, but I wanted to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any kind, witness, about the military field or about explosives? I'm not just talking about ballistics. Or do you have knowledge of any other kind? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, madam, are you aware of the conclusions reached in this report at the time?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll go back to that question because I'm not sure of what I heard. At the time that your report was written, your expert report, were you aware of the existence of this UN report and were you aware of the gist of its conclusions; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I didn't have it in my possession. I simply heard about it when it was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I know that you didn't have these document, but my question is as follows, madam: It's possible not to have a document but nevertheless be familiar with certain things. Were you familiar with the conclusions in general terms of this report? That is all I want to ask you. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now go back to page 73 and 74. You answered some of the Prosecution's questions about the interior, and you said perhaps that it was worse than the exterior, according to the author that you quoted. My question is as follows: With regard to this interior blockade, were you personally aware of events in Sarajevo which could be the basis for your conclusions? And if so, what were these events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was this basis?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This does not arise from cross-examination. I did not ask questions from the interior blockade, details about it, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked about the basis for the conclusions that the interior blockade was worse than the exterior blockade, so the Defence is entitled to further investigate the reasons for this conclusion. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, but could you please finish in a couple of minutes. But objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll make an effort to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, you heard the question. Could you please answer the question. What was your personal experience?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you did experience this. What can you tell us -- what can you tell the Trial Chamber? What did you see? What did you find out about? What did you feel, learn, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: Do you mean when I was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to the interior blockade. Yes, in fact that's it.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I managed to take down the notes from the conversation with the Muslim man who throughout the military operation lived in Sarajevo and is living there nowadays as well. In my book, I reported his entire story, and he said in great detail what sufferings he went through, and not just him but the non-Muslim population, what they had to suffer through during the war. And that is very important, and this is something that I conveyed in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But what do you yourself know? What examples could you provide us with? And I think that will be my last question.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA
utterances.text: I spoke with people who left Sarajevo with great difficulty but left, with people who paid their way out, and all of this created a general impression on how difficult it was for the non-Muslim population in Sarajevo, regardless of how few of them there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may confer for 30 seconds. No more, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say two words while we're having a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps if the parties are conferring, I'd rather not ask you to because they could not pay proper attention to your words. What would you like to say, Ms. Guskova? Yes, Madam Guskova asked whether she could say two words. I would allow her. Would you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And perhaps she could say a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Guskova, we are not yet at the end of your testimony. So if it would be any comments, perhaps leave it to the end. If it is, however, something we should know about at this moment, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I simply wanted to fill up the break we were having. But I can wait until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are no further questions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Guskova, since the Bench have a few questions for you as well and since that will certainly take more than three, four, or five minutes, we'll have to adjourn now, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, not in this courtroom but in Courtroom II. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony -- about the testimony you have given until now and the testimony you are still about to give, and I'll ask Mr. Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Meanwhile, I will invite the parties to return to me as well page 2251, which is the fourth page of the translation I was so kind to provide to the parties, so that my copy is complete again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hope I'm not suspected of an ulterior motive, but I don't believe I received the last page, if the fourth page is the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least let's -- perhaps it is on my desk so I would then have to apologise. But if page 4 is missing, we'll find it. I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is in the hands of the witness now, I think. The witness should not leave with your documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any documents in the hands of the witness at this very moment -- Yes. Madam Guskova, we're just wondering where -- we're just wondering whether there's still one of the documents provided to you by either the Chamber or the parties in your possession. I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was suggested by the Defence that you might have one. So we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning. I think the B/C/S version is with Madam Registrar at this very moment. So I suggest to the parties that I'll take back the B/C/S version as well and that we work on a copy that will be provided overnight of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you're welcome to take the fourth page of the copy we found shortly after you brought this to light or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's with the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: ERN number. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- As mine, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit 1. Yes, that's page 2251. Thank you very much for returning it. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
